title: The cool clouds of Carina
caption: Cold dust clouds in the Carina Nebula, imaged by APEX and the Curtis Schmidt telescope
celestial: Carina Nebula, NGC 3372 · constellation Carina · about 7500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO/APEX/T. Preibisch et al. (Submillimetre); N. Smith, University of Minnesota/NOAO/AURA/NSF (Optical)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Orange tones trace the cold, dusty clouds of the Carina Nebula, where stars form, laid over a visible-light view of the region. The orange layer comes from the APEX telescope and its LABOCA camera, observing submillimeter light at a wavelength of 870 µm. The visible-light picture was taken with the Curtis Schmidt telescope, which stands at Cerro Tololo Interamerican Observatory.

The Carina Nebula is a site of violent star formation and home to some of the most massive stars in our galaxy. That makes it a good place to study how young stars interact with the molecular clouds they were born from.

The numbers are large. The nebula contains stars adding up to more than 25 000 Suns, and its clouds of gas and dust hold about 140 000 Suns' worth of mass. Cold dust gives off little visible light but glows at submillimeter wavelengths, which is why APEX can map it.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (68.10 x 76.98 arcminutes) and distance (7500 light years), the frame spans roughly 149 × 168 light-years. Its light set out about 7,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: APEX's LABOCA camera recorded cold dust at a submillimeter wavelength of 870 µm, shown in orange, over a visible-light image from the Curtis Schmidt telescope.
understand.eye: Submillimeter light is invisible to the eye, so the orange clouds show cold dust that cannot be seen directly.
